Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Energy | International COP31: Advocates urge funders to double clean air money for Africa, Asia and Latin America by COP32 Source : Michael Asharley | Clean Air Beat Journalist 17 November 2026 2:50pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Clean air advocates at COP31 have urged philanthropic funders to double their annual support for air quality initiatives in Africa, Latin America and parts of Asia, warning that inadequate financing is undermining efforts to tackle pollution in some of the world's most affected regions.
The advocates say the three regions, excluding China and India, currently receive a combined US$8.3 million annually in philanthropic funding for clean air work.
They want that amount increased to about US$16 million a year, with more resources directed towards locally led monitoring systems, research and the use of air quality data in policymaking.
The call was made during a session on financing clean air in the Global South, co-hosted by Sustenta Honduras and Clean Energy Nepal in Antalya, Türkiye, on November 13.
Opening the session, Sustenta Honduras Executive Director Ricardo said the discussion was intended to demonstrate how locally generated air quality data could influence public policy and government spending.
“We want to show what implementation looks like when air quality data produced in country reaches the people who set the policies and budget,” he said.
Christa Hasenkopf, Director of the Clean Air Program and Founder of the EPIC Air Quality Fund at the University of Chicago’s Energy Policy Institute, said fine particulate matter pollution (PM2.5) contributes to about eight million deaths annually and is the world's second-leading health risk factor, behind high blood pressure.
She cited World Bank estimates that the health damage associated with PM2.5 pollution costs the global economy about US$8.1 trillion.
Despite the scale of the problem, Hasenkopf said less than 0.1 per cent of global philanthropic funding goes towards clean air initiatives, citing the Clean Air Fund.
“If you look at Africa, it receives less than a million dollars a year on average for clean air work. Yet PM2.5 kills more folks than HIV/AIDS, or malaria,” she said.
International development funding is also limited. The Clean Air Fund’s State of Global Air Quality Funding 2026 report found that less than one per cent of international development funding is directed specifically towards outdoor air pollution.
The report also found that 89 per cent of air quality funding between 2020 and 2024 was provided as loans.
However, a report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition, Hidden Assets , estimates that every US$1 invested in measures addressing air pollution and climate change together generates about US$15 in returns.
Hasenkopf challenged funders to help close the financing gap before the next climate summit.
“If you look at philanthropic funding for clean air in Asia excluding China and India, Africa and Latin America combined, it's US$8.3 million a year. We can double that,” she said.
She said the immediate target was to raise annual funding for the three regions to about US$16 million, arguing that a small number of major funders could help achieve the increase.
“Probably just a couple funders … could double that amount across the world and it’d be incredibly meaningful,” she said, suggesting that grants of between US$50,000 and US$100,000 per project would be a useful starting point.
Hasenkopf also stressed that funding should strengthen air quality monitoring capacity in the countries affected by pollution rather than leave them dependent on external programmes.
She cited a US State Department initiative that installed air quality monitors at diplomatic missions in 38 countries and, according to research, contributed to reductions in PM2.5 levels.
Following the programme's abrupt closure last year, she said, 97 per cent of reference-grade monitors disappeared in countries prioritised by the EPIC Air Quality Fund. She added that a study found pollution levels subsequently increased.
“Someone else’s monitors operate on someone else’s priorities. Air quality infrastructure persists when it’s owned by the country that’s breathing the air,” she said.
Established in 2024, the EPIC Air Quality Fund now supports 70 awardees in 44 countries, providing grants of between US$50,000 and US$75,000 over 18 months.
Hasenkopf said the fund had recorded an 80 per cent increase in open air quality monitoring data in Africa during its first 18 months, alongside 16 national policy impacts.
She cited The Gambia as an example of how locally generated data could influence policy. The country, which she said had no air quality monitoring three years ago, now has data that helped inform the drafting of its first air quality standards.
The data was collected by a pulmonologist and a colleague, and the standards have since been passed by Parliament, she said.
In Honduras, Sustenta Honduras Communications Lead Baleria Savion said the organisation had expanded air quality monitoring from two major cities to more than 60 locations across the country.
She said the EPIC Air Quality Fund had ranked Honduras third among 147 countries for air quality data gaps in 2023.
“Air quality is actually the leading cause of death in our country and it reduces life expectancy by two and a half years,” Savion said.
“Before we only had monitors in two of the main cities, but now we have more than 60 across the territory.”
She said national media outlets had begun using data from the network because it was the only available source of information on air quality in several areas.
Savion added that a member of Congress had pledged to introduce an air quality law, which the organisation hopes will be achieved by 2027.
Clean Energy Nepal Programme Coordinator Prakash Lama said the country's annual average PM2.5 concentration had been reported at 51.7 micrograms per cubic metre, approximately 10 times the World Health Organization's recommended guideline.
He cited a government study that attributed about 42,000 deaths to air pollution, including 26,000 premature deaths annually, and estimated the economic cost at more than six per cent of Nepal's gross domestic product.
Lama said the challenge extended beyond the absence of policies or monitoring infrastructure to the availability and continuity of reliable data.
His organisation has deployed 20 sensors across 10 cities to complement government monitoring and submitted recommendations on Nepal's proposed national PM2.5 standard.
He called for dedicated climate financing for air quality initiatives, warning that the issue should not remain an underfunded development priority.
Deo Okure, Head of Research and Global Partnerships at AirQo and co-facilitator of the Africa Clean Air Network (AfriCAN), said the organisation operates more than 600 monitors across over 16 African cities.
He estimated that Africa has about 2,000 active air quality monitors, compared with approximately 10,000 active reference stations in the United States.
Okure questioned the extent to which funding commitments announced at successive climate summits translate into resources for communities and countries most affected by pollution.
“Almost every COP brings some sort of funding commitments but … very little of that translates into what you would see that could catalyze action at local levels or in … countries that are most affected,” he said.
He also cautioned against treating open air quality data as cost-free, pointing out that monitoring infrastructure, data collection and analysis require sustained investment.
“When you say open data it doesn’t mean free data. Someone has paid for it,” he said.
Okure urged funders to support less visible but essential areas of the work, including technical and institutional capacity development.
Teddy Nabakooza Galiwango, Principal Environmental Officer of Uganda’s Kingdom of Buganda, said investment in monitoring should be accompanied by efforts to ensure that data informs practical interventions.
“Expansion of data monitoring, but as we do that, it’s important to strengthen the pathway from data to action,” she said.
Savion proposed a minimum target for the next year, urging stakeholders to ensure that every country has at least one air quality monitor providing publicly accessible data.
“By next year we should make sure all countries have at least one air quality monitor that provides open access to that data,” she said.
